summary: Reviewed terminal WebSocket backend and stopwatch widget API. Terminal has HIGH-severity command injection in dispatch endpoint. Stopwatch API is LOW-risk (simple CRUD, no auth but local-only). CORS misconfiguration persists. XSS protections properly implemented.

findings: Simple CRUD operations on JSON file - no injection vectors
8-character UUID IDs (low entropy but acceptable for stopwatches)
No authentication (acceptable for local-only personal widget)
concerns: No rate limiting on create - could create many stopwatches
Label field not sanitized but rendered with escapeHtml() in frontend
stopwatch_review.verdict: Approved for deployment. Stopwatch feature is safe for local use.

vulnerabilities.description: The dispatch_agent() endpoint builds a shell command by escaping double quotes and newlines in the prompt, but this is insufficient. The escape pattern `prompt.replace('"', '\"')` does not handle shell metacharacters like $(), backticks, semicolons, pipes, or ampersands. An attacker can inject arbitrary commands via the prompt parameter.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Use subprocess with arguments list instead of shell command string. Replace the command construction with proper argument passing that doesn't go through shell interpretation.

vulnerabilities.description: The terminal WebSocket and all REST endpoints lack authentication. Anyone with access to localhost:7777 can: create terminal sessions, send keystrokes to terminals, spawn shell processes, execute arbitrary commands via dispatch. Combined with CORS *, any webpage can connect via JavaScript.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Implement WebSocket authentication via Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header token or first-message auth handshake. Add API key middleware to all terminal REST endpoints. Consider rate limiting session creation.

vulnerabilities.description: CORS is configured with allow_origins=['*'] and allow_credentials=True. This permits any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to the API, including WebSocket upgrade requests. While the server binds to 127.0.0.1, browser-based attacks from malicious websites can still reach localhost.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Restrict allow_origins to specific trusted origins only (e.g., ['http://localhost:7777', 'chrome-extension://<id>']). Consider removing allow_credentials if not needed.

vulnerabilities.description: The cwd parameter in create_session() is user-controllable and is passed directly to subprocess. While Python's subprocess.Popen does validate the path exists, there's no validation to restrict terminals to safe directories. An attacker could create a terminal with cwd='C:\Windows\System32' or any other sensitive directory.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Validate cwd against an allowlist of safe directories or ensure it's within the workspace project root. Add path canonicalization to prevent ../ traversal.

vulnerabilities.description: WebSocket endpoint auto-creates sessions if session_id doesn't exist. An attacker could predict or brute-force session IDs (8 character UUIDs) to hijack or pre-create sessions. Session IDs use only first 8 chars of UUID which reduces entropy to 32 bits.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Use full UUID for session IDs. Don't auto-create sessions on WebSocket connect - require explicit session creation via POST first. Add session ownership validation.

vulnerabilities.description: Terminal sessions persist indefinitely with no idle timeout. Shell processes remain alive consuming resources. An attacker could spawn many sessions leading to resource exhaustion.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Implement idle session timeout (e.g., 30 minutes). Add maximum concurrent sessions limit. Clean up sessions on server shutdown.

vulnerabilities.description: No rate limiting on session creation, dispatch, or resize endpoints. An attacker can spawn unlimited terminal sessions or flood the server with requests causing denial of service.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Add rate limiting middleware (e.g., slowapi). Limit session creation to reasonable rate. Consider per-IP limits.

vulnerabilities.description: Exception messages are returned directly to clients (str(e)). This could leak internal paths, Python tracebacks, or system information.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Log full errors server-side. Return generic error messages to clients.

vulnerabilities.description: WebSocket URLs are hardcoded as 'ws://localhost:7777/...'. Minor coupling issue.
vulnerabilities.recommendation: Construct WebSocket URL dynamically from request headers.

positive_findings: Server binds to 127.0.0.1 only in run.py and run_silent.py (not exposed to network)
XSS protection via escapeHtml() is properly implemented and used consistently
Frontend uses SRI hashes on CDN imports for xterm.js (integrity verification)
Pydantic models used for request validation (type checking)
Scrollback buffer has fixed size (1000 lines) preventing memory exhaustion
Process termination has timeout handling to prevent zombie processes
No secrets or API keys found in code
Frontend action rendering properly escapes user-controlled content
pii_handling: Terminal scrollback stores raw command output which may contain PII
No PII redaction in logs or scrollback buffer

owasp_summary.A01_Broken_Access_Control: HIGH - No auth on terminal endpoints
owasp_summary.A02_Cryptographic_Failures: N/A - No encryption required for local-only service
owasp_summary.A03_Injection: HIGH - Command injection in dispatch endpoint
owasp_summary.A04_Insecure_Design: MEDIUM - Missing session timeouts and rate limiting
owasp_summary.A06_Vulnerable_Components: LOW - CDN dependencies have SRI hashes
owasp_summary.A07_Auth_Failures: MEDIUM - Weak session IDs, no ownership validation
owasp_summary.A09_Logging_Failures: MEDIUM - No audit logging for terminal commands
owasp_summary.A10_SSRF: N/A - No outbound requests based on user input

blockers.reason: Command injection in dispatch endpoint allows arbitrary code execution
Unauthenticated terminal access is effectively a remote shell

approval_conditions: Implement authentication (SEC-002) before any network exposure
handoff_notes: @backend-dev: SEC-001 is critical command injection. The escape logic in dispatch_agent() is insufficient - shell metacharacters like $(), backticks, semicolons bypass it. Use subprocess args list, not shell string. SEC-002 requires auth - consider FastAPI Depends() with API key header. @frontend-dev: XSS protections look good. Add reconnection error handling for when auth is implemented. @devops: DO NOT deploy terminal until SEC-001 and SEC-002 are fixed.
